knowledge: Intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (IDDFBA; OMIM #618089) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by heterozygous de novo loss-of-function or missense variants in FBXO11. The hallmark description was defined primarily by Gregor et al. (2018, PMID: 30100085), characterizing individuals with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, prominent language impairment, behavioral issues (such as ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, and aggressive behaviors), and distinct craniofacial features (including frontal bossing, hypertelorism/telecanthus, broad nasal tip/bridge, and thin upper lip).
prior_hypothesis: A patient with FBXO11-related disorder cannot be uniquely diagnosed purely on a single pathognomonic sign; however, they can be differentiated from clinically overlapping syndromes by a combination of profound speech delay disproportionate to motor delay, severe externalizing behavioral disturbances (ADHD, impulsive/aggressive behaviors, sleep problems), and facial dysmorphisms (prominent forehead, broad/bulbous nasal tip, thin upper vermilion, and downslanting palpebral fissures), coupled with the distinct absence of progressive microcephaly, coarse facial features, severe visceral malformations, or hypoplastic distal phalanges/nails.

candidate_answers.answer: In the index cohort reported by Gregor et al. 2018 (PMID: 30100085), speech and language impairment (HP:0000750) is near-universal (~100%, 14/14 individuals assessed), frequently presenting as absent speech or significant expressive language delay compared to motor milestones.

Behavioral abnormalities (HP:0000708) including hyperactivity/ADHD (HP:0007018), aggressive behavior (HP:0000718), and autistic traits or ASD (HP:0000729) are reported in approximately 70-80% of individuals in initial cohorts (e.g., Gregor et al. 2018), serving as key clinical features separating it from quiet or hypoactive syndromic ID presentations.

Recurrent craniofacial dysmorphisms include prominent forehead/frontal bossing (HP:0002007), broad nasal tip (HP:0000455), hypertelorism (HP:0000316) or telecanthus (HP:0000506), and thin upper lip vermilion (HP:0000219), present in >60-75% of reported cases in Gregor et al. 2018.

Discrimination against Coffin-Siris syndrome (ARID1B and related genes) relies on the absence of hypoplastic or absent fifth fingernails/toenails (HP:0001792/HP:0001800) and lack of generalized hypertrichosis (HP:0000998) in FBXO11 patients; discrimination against Koolen-de Vries syndrome (KANSL1) relies on the absence of a characteristic pear-shaped nose and hyper-affable personality.

Features that are consistently absent or rare (acting as negative discriminators) include progressive neurodegeneration, structural congenital limb-reduction deficiencies, complex congenital heart defects, and persistent profound microcephaly (head circumference is typically normal to mildly macrocephalic).

Most variants represent haploinsufficiency via de novo loss-of-function (frameshift, nonsense, canonical splice site mutations), while missense variants clustering in critical functional domains (such as the F-box or UBR domains) yield an indistinguishable core phenotype without proven distinct genotype-phenotype divergence to date.

key_terms: Intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities
open_questions: What are the precise numerators and denominators for each dysmorphic trait and behavioral symptom across all published FBXO11 cases since 2018?

Do individuals harboring missense variants in specific functional domains of FBXO11 exhibit a milder or distinct phenotype compared to those with whole-gene deletions or truncating loss-of-function mutations?
Are there any documented conflicting clinical findings regarding seizures or structural brain anomalies (e.g., corpus callosum hypoplasia) between early and recent cohorts?
assumptions: OMIM #618089 represents a single disease entity caused by heterozygous loss-of-function or pathogenic missense variants in FBXO11.
The primary clinical series establishing initial numerators and denominators is Gregor et al. 2018 (PMID: 30100085), supplemented by small subsequent case reports.
The clinician is evaluating constitutional germline pediatric and young adult presentations where phenotypic comparisons against common syndromic ID differential diagnoses are required.
